title: Create an account and sign in
summary: How to create an account on Blipmade, confirm the address and open the first session.

blocks.text: An account holds your services, your domains, your invoices and your support tickets. The registration asks for your first name, your last name, the address of your email and a password.

items.title: Fill in the registration form
items.body: Open the page Create account and fill in the fields First name, Last name, Email address and Password.
items.result: The form refuses an address that another account already uses and a password that does not meet the rules.

items.title: Confirm the address
items.body: Open the message that the platform sent to the address of the account and follow the link of the message.
items.result: The address is confirmed and the page offers the button Go to your dashboard.

items.title: Sign in
items.body: Open the sign-in page, write your address and your password and sign in.
items.result: The dashboard of your account opens.

blocks.text: The sign-in page and the page of the forgotten password answer the same way for every address, so they never say whether an account exists.
The password is checked before it is accepted, and the form writes down what is missing.

rows.v: At least 10 characters, and at most 200.
At least one lowercase letter and one uppercase letter.
At least one number.

blocks.text: A password manager is the easiest way to hold a long password that follows the rules.
There is no API of keys today. A program that talks to the platform uses the session of an account.

sections.title: Sign in, sign out and the sessions

blocks.text: A session lasts fourteen days and is not extended by the activity. When it ends, the page asks you to sign in again. You can see the open sessions of the account and close them at any time from the settings.

items.q: I forgot the password.
items.a: Open the sign-in page, follow the link called 'Forgot password?' and use the link of the message that arrives. Choosing a new password ends every session of the account, including the one on your phone.

items.q: The page says that the email address or the password is not correct.
items.a: The address and the password are checked together, so the message does not tell you which of the two is wrong. Check the address and try again, or follow the link called 'Forgot password?' under the password field.

items.q: I do not receive the message with the confirmation link.
items.a: Look in the folder of the junk mail and in the folder of the spam. If the message does not arrive, ask for a new link on the sign-in page or open a support ticket.

blocks.text: The dashboard of the account shows the services you have, the catalog of the products and the state of your invoices. The first step is to order an application.

Read [Deploy your first app](/docs?p=first-app) next. [The dashboard of your account](/docs?p=dashboard) tells you where everything is, and [Your profile, your address and your sessions](/docs?p=account) tells you what you can change about the account.

title: Deploy your first app
summary: How to order an application, what you find in the container and how to open the service.

blocks.text: The catalog holds the apps and the databases that can be ordered. Every entry carries its own resources and its own price.

items.title: Pick the product
items.body: Open Deploy in the menu and pick the product in the catalog. The card of the product shows the memory, the vCPU and the storage it needs.
items.result: The page of the product opens with the resources and the price of the entry.

items.title: Choose the resources
items.body: Give the instance a name, choose the memory, the vCPU and the storage, and choose the options you want. The estimate follows every change.
items.result: The button Review order is available.

items.title: Review the order
items.body: Check the configuration and the price of the order and choose Continue to payment.
items.result: The page of the payment opens.

items.title: Place the order
items.body: Choose Pay and deploy.
items.result: The platform starts the deployment and the page shows the steps of it.

items.title: Open the instance
items.body: When the deployment is finished, choose Open instance.
items.result: The page of the instance opens with the tabs of the service.

blocks.text: Payments are not available yet. Your order is created and stays unpaid, so open a support ticket and we finish the payment with you.

sections.title: What the deployment writes into the container

blocks.text: A deployment writes a minimal Node.js application into the container and starts it with npm run start. The container runs the Node.js image of the platform.

The application answers on the health path of the product with a small JSON document that carries the name of the product, the state and the time the container has been running. Every other path answers with a line of text that names the product.
The product itself is not installed by the platform yet. What runs in the container until you put your own files there is a minimal application of the platform.

items.title: Open the address of the instance
items.body: The address of the instance is on the page of the instance. Open it in a browser.
items.result: The application answers with the code 200.

items.title: Read the output of the container
items.body: Open the tab Console of the instance. The output of the container is written there, and the field Command lets you send a command to the service.
items.result: You see the line that says the application listens on the port of the allocation.

blocks.text: The platform writes three files into the container: package.json, index.js and README.md. The README.md of the container says that the code of the product replaces them.

sections.title: If the service does not answer

items.q: The address does not answer at all.
items.a: Check that the instance is started: the tab Overview shows the state and the buttons Start, Restart and Stop. Then open the tab Console and read the output of the container.

items.q: The deployment failed.
items.a: A deployment that could not be delivered is refunded by the platform, and the event is written in the events of the instance. See [Refunds and credits](/docs?p=refunds).

items.q: My application answers on another port.
items.a: The container has to listen on the port of its allocation; the port of the allocation is given to the container in SERVER_PORT. An application that listens on another port is served to nobody.

items: Put your own code in the container: [the files of the instance](/docs?p=files).
Give the service an address of your own: [Domains and SSL](/docs?p=domains).
Keep a copy of the files: [Backups](/docs?p=backups).
Change the size of the service when it needs more: [Choose the right resources](/docs?p=resources).

title: Your profile, your address and your sessions
summary: What the settings of the account hold and how to change the name, the address, the password and the sessions.

blocks.text: The settings of the account hold the name, the address and the password. Everything else of the account has a page of its own: the services, the domains, the invoices and the tickets.

rows.v: The first part of the name. The platform writes it in the messages it sends you.
The second part of the name of the account.
The address where the platform writes to you. A new address is only used after the link of the confirmation.
The role of the account on the platform. The account you create yourself is a customer account.

blocks.text: The address of the account is also where the platform writes about your services: a deployment that is finished, an invoice, a change of resources that was refused.

sections.title: Change the address of the account

items.title: Open the settings
items.body: Choose Settings in the menu and open the panel Profile.
items.result: The fields of the account appear.

items.title: Write the new address
items.body: Fill in the field New email address and send the form.
items.result: The platform writes a confirmation link to the new address. The account keeps the old address until the link is used.

items.title: Confirm the new address
items.body: Open the message that arrives at the new address and follow the link of the message.
items.result: The new address is the address of the account.

blocks.text: An address that another account already uses is refused. Only one request is open at a time: a new request replaces the one that is waiting for its confirmation.

items.title: Open the settings
items.body: Choose Settings in the menu and open the panel Password.
items.result: The fields Current password, New password and Repeat the new password appear.

items.title: Write the new password
items.body: Fill in the three fields and save the form.
items.result: The password of the account is changed.

blocks.text: The sessions of the other devices end with the change. The session you are using stays, so you are not signed out of the page you are on.
The rules of the password are the same as when the account was created: at least ten characters, a lowercase letter, an uppercase letter and a number.
The panel Sessions lists the sessions that are open for the account, with the device and the date of each one. The session you are in is marked with This device.
A session lasts fourteen days and is not extended by the activity. You can end one session, or all the other sessions at once.
A session you do not know is a reason to change the password. The change ends the other sessions of the account.
The panel Account of the settings closes the account. The platform asks for your password and for the words CLOSE MY ACCOUNT, so a request is never made by mistake.
The request is recorded. Your services keep running until the end of the period you paid for, and the team writes to you before anything is closed. A request can be taken back while it is open.
Closing the account is not the same as cancelling an instance. The data of a cancelled instance is kept for the term of retention: see [Cancel an instance](/docs?p=cancel).

title: The dashboard of your account
summary: What the pages of the dashboard show and where the actions of the platform are.

blocks.text: The menu of the dashboard holds the same eight entries on every screen:

items: Overview — the state of the account: the services, what needs your attention and the last events.
Deploy — the catalog of the apps and the databases that can be ordered.
Apps & databases — the services you have, with the state of each one.
Domains — the hostnames of your services and their certificates.
Email — the mailboxes of the platform and the hosted mail.
Billing — the estimate of the month, the subscriptions and the invoices.
Support — the tickets you opened and the answers of the team.
Settings — the profile, the address, the password, the sessions and the notifications.

blocks.text: The Overview page is the first screen after the sign-in. It carries a tile for the number of your services (Services), the total of the month (Monthly total), the services that need you (Needs attention) and the way into the catalog (Deploy).

items: Deploy your first app — the panel that is there when you have no service yet.
Needs attention — the services that need you: a service whose status is failed, degraded or suspended, and a service whose subscription payment is past due.
Your services — the list of your instances, with the state of each one.
Recent activity — the last event of every service.

blocks.text: Every service opens on a page of its own. The tabs are the same for every product:

items: Overview — the state, the address and the actions of the service.
Console — the output of the container and the field to send a command.
Files — the file browser of the container.
Databases — the databases that belong to the instance.
Backups — the copies of the files that you made.
Network — the address and the port of the service.
Startup — the image, the command and the environment of the container.
Schedules — the tasks that run in the container.
Settings — the name of the instance and the cancellation.
Activity — the events of the instance.
Resources — the memory, the vCPU and the storage of the instance.
Domains — the hostnames that point at the instance.

title: WordPress
summary: What you get today when you order WordPress, and what the platform does not install yet.

blocks.text: WordPress is the most widely used content management system. It is a PHP application that needs a web server, a PHP runtime and a database of its own.
A deployment of WordPress writes a minimal Node.js application into the container and starts it with npm run start. The container runs the Node.js image of the platform.

{{planned}} WordPress itself is not installed today. When it is, the instance will run a WordPress installation with its own PHP, its own web server and its own database. Until then, what runs in the container is a minimal application of the platform.

The product page of the catalog shows the entry: the category, the minimum of resources and the price. The deploy page carries the state of the entry: an entry that cannot be ordered says so there and the order is blocked.

sections.title: Read the output of the service

blocks.text: The tab Console of the instance shows the output of the container as it is written, and the field Command lets you send a command to the service. The state of the console is written at the top of the panel: Connected, Connecting or Disconnected.
The platform does not keep a history of the output. If your application has to keep a log of its own, write it to a file of the container and read it in the tab Files.
The backups are made by you, on demand, from the tab Backups of the instance. The platform copies the files of the container into an archive that you can download and restore.
Nothing makes a backup on a schedule and the platform keeps no history of them. Take a backup before you change something big in the container.
A backup is a copy of the files of the container, not the export of the instance. See [Cancel an instance](/docs?p=cancel).

sections.title: When the service does not answer

items.q: The container answers, but I expected WordPress.
items.a: The deployment writes the application of the platform, not WordPress. Put the files of your WordPress installation in the container yourself, and check that the container runs the image and the command that your installation needs.

items.q: The address answers with a line of text instead of my site.
items.a: That line is the answer of the application of the platform. It stays as long as the files of the platform are the ones that run.

items.q: My WordPress installation does not start.
items.a: The container runs Node.js. A WordPress installation needs PHP and a web server, and the platform does not provide them in the container today. Read the output of the container in the tab Console to see what the start command says.

blocks.text: MongoDB is a document database: it keeps the documents of an application and answers the queries of the application over the network.
MongoDB cannot be ordered today: the platform does not offer it yet. This page shows what it will be when it is.
A deployment of MongoDB writes a minimal Node.js application into the container and starts it with npm run start, exactly like every other product.

{{planned}} MongoDB itself is not installed today. When it is, the instance will run a MongoDB server in the container. Until then, what runs in the container is a minimal application of the platform.

The product page of the catalog shows the entry: the category, the minimum of resources and the price. The deploy page carries the state of the entry: an entry that cannot be ordered says so there and the order is blocked.

sections.title: A database that belongs to your instance

blocks.text: A database that belongs to an instance is created in the tab Databases of the instance page. The platform keeps it on the node of the instance, so it is not a server that runs inside the container.

items.title: Open the tab Databases
items.body: Open the instance and choose the tab Databases.
items.result: The tab Databases shows the databases that belong to the instance.

items.title: Create the database
items.body: Fill in the fields Name of the database, User of the database and Password, and leave the allowed address as it is if the connection comes from the instance itself.
items.result: The database appears in the list of the tab.

items.title: Take the credentials
items.body: Choose Credentials to see the host, the port, the user and the password of the database.
items.result: The dialog says: Copy them now. The password can be asked for again, but every ask is written to the log.

blocks.text: The databases of an instance are its own. They are not shared with the other instances of the account.

sections.title: Connect your code to the database

blocks.text: The platform sets no environment variable that you have to fill in. The tab Startup of the instance shows it in these words: No variables. The container starts without any environment variable.
The connection details of a database are yours to write: you write them in your code, or in the tab Startup of the instance with Add a variable, and you use them there.

The host of a database of an instance is the address that the tab Databases shows. Your application runs in the container, so the host has to be reachable from there: the allowed address of the database decides who may open a connection to it.
The backups are made by you, on demand, from the tab Backups of the instance. The platform copies the files of the container into an archive that you can download and restore.
Nothing makes a backup on a schedule and the platform keeps no history of them.
A backup holds the files of the container. The data of a database is not part of it, so copy the data you cannot lose yourself.

sections.title: Change the size of the service

blocks.text: The tab Resources of the instance shows the memory, the vCPU and the storage that the service has, and the price of the month.
A change of resources is an order that has to be paid, and the service is restarted when the change is applied. Read [Upgrade or resize an instance](/docs?p=upgrade) before you change anything.

sections.title: When the service does not answer

items.q: I cannot order MongoDB.
items.a: MongoDB cannot be ordered today: the platform does not offer it yet. When it is, the order can be placed from the page of the product.

items.q: My application cannot reach the database.
items.a: A database of an instance is kept on the node of the instance, and the allowed address of the database decides who may open a connection to it. Check the host in the tab Databases and the address you allowed.

items.q: The container answers, but there is no database in it.
items.a: The deployment writes the application of the platform. The database server of the product is not installed in the container today.

title: Choose the right resources
summary: What the memory, the vCPU and the storage of an instance mean and how the price follows them.

blocks.text: An instance runs in a container with three limits. The container gets exactly what you buy, and the limits are the limits of the service until a change of resources is applied.

rows.v: The memory the container may use. The interface shows it in MB or in GB.
The number of processors the container may use.
The space of the disk of the container. The files you upload take that space.

blocks.text: The minimum and the maximum belong to the product in the catalog. A configuration under the minimum or over the maximum is refused.

sections.title: How the price follows the resources

blocks.text: The price of a configuration is calculated by the platform from the resources you choose. The price is in euros and the period is the month.

Every product of the catalog carries a minimum of resources and a price of its own. The page of the product shows the minimum in the panel Minimum resources, and the card of the product in the catalog shows the starting price.
The tab Resources of an instance shows what you bought: the purchased limits, the price of the month and, when a change is being prepared, the price the change would bring.

sections.title: Change the resources of an instance

items.title: Open the tab Resources
items.body: Open the instance and choose the tab Resources. The purchased limits and the price of the month are there.
items.result: The fields of the memory, the vCPU and the storage are filled in with what the service has.

items.title: Write the new values
items.body: Change the three values and choose Save resources.
items.result: The platform shows the price of the change: the new price and the difference.

items.title: Pay for the change
items.body: A change that costs more is an order that has to be paid before it touches the service.
items.result: The service keeps the limits it has until the order is settled.

blocks.text: A change that costs less is settled by the platform itself, and the difference is carried to the next invoice. The service is restarted when a change is applied.
Read [Upgrade or resize an instance](/docs?p=upgrade) for the whole of the change.

sections.title: What a change does not touch

items: The files of the container stay as they are.
The hostnames of the instance stay pointed at the same port.
The databases of the instance stay where they are.

items.q: The minimum of the product is not enough for my application.
items.a: The minimum is the smallest configuration the catalog allows for this product, and the platform refuses a configuration that is under it. Change the product, or put the application on an instance of a product with a smaller minimum.

items.q: The price of my instance did not change with the resources.
items.a: A change that costs more is applied when the order is paid, and a change that costs less is carried to the next invoice. The price of the month follows the limits that the service really has.

items.q: Can I change only the storage?
items.a: The three values are always sent together: a change carries the memory, the vCPU and the storage of the service.

title: Invoices and payment methods
summary: What the billing page shows, when an invoice is written and how a payment is made today.

items: This month (estimate) — the sum of the prices of the services you have today.
Current period ends — the day your current period ends.
Payment method — the method on the account, with the action Manage payment method.
Subscriptions — one subscription per instance, with the period, the state, the amount and the action Cancel at period end.
Invoices — the invoices of the account, with the number, the date, the amount, the state and the link to the invoice.

blocks.text: An invoice is written when a period is paid. It carries a number, the amount, the tax and the state, and the newest is at the top of the list. The state of an invoice is one of Draft, Open, Paid, Void or Uncollectible.
The column Invoice opens the invoice of the provider. An invoice that has no link shows a dash; the amount is on the page in every case.
Before the first payment there is no invoice: the page shows the estimate of the month.
Payments are not available yet. Your order is created and stays unpaid, so open a support ticket and we finish the payment with you.
The whole chain is in place — the order, the subscription, the invoice, the deployment and the message that tells you it is done — but the payment itself is finished with the team.
The action Manage payment method opens the billing portal of the provider. It stays disabled while a payment cannot be taken, and the reason is written under the button.

items.q: I do not see an invoice for my instance.
items.a: An invoice is written when a period is paid. Before that, the page shows the estimate of the month in This month (estimate).

items.q: The estimate of the month is not the amount of my invoice.
items.a: The estimate is the sum of the prices of the services you have today. An invoice is the price of one period that was paid.

items.q: I cannot pay my invoice.
items.a: The platform cannot take a payment today. Open a ticket from the menu Support and the team finishes the payment with you.

title: Upgrade or resize an instance
summary: How a change of resources is ordered, what it costs and when it is applied.

sections.title: A change of resources is an order

blocks.text: The resources of an instance are not changed on the spot. A change is an order that has to be paid, and the service keeps the resources it has until the order is settled.

items: An increase is applied when the order is paid.
A decrease is settled by the platform itself, and the difference is carried to the next invoice.
The service is restarted when a change is applied.

blocks.text: The resources of a service that has not been paid for are never changed.

items.title: Open the tab Resources
items.body: Open the instance and choose the tab Resources.
items.result: The purchased limits and the price of the month are there.

items.title: Write the new values
items.body: Change the memory, the vCPU or the storage and choose Save resources.
items.result: The platform shows the price of the change: the new price and the difference.

items.title: Pay the difference
items.body: When the change costs more, the platform writes an order for it and asks for the payment. The service is not touched before the payment.
items.result: The order carries a number and is written in the events of the instance.

items.title: Watch the change
items.body: An increase is applied as soon as the order is paid. A decrease is settled by the platform and lowers the amount of the next invoice.
items.result: The tab Resources shows the limits that the service really has.

sections.title: When the change cannot be applied

blocks.text: If the platform cannot apply a change that was paid for, the money goes back to you by itself: the order is marked as refunded and the instance keeps the resources it had. The event is written in the tab Activity of the instance.
A change that was never paid for is simply not applied. There is nothing to refund, because the money was never taken.
See [Refunds and credits](/docs?p=refunds) for the whole of the subject.

items.q: Do I lose my files when I change the resources?
items.a: No. A change of resources touches the limits of the container: the files, the hostnames and the databases of the instance stay as they are.

items.q: Can I change the resources without paying?
items.a: No. A change of resources is an order that has to be paid: an increase is applied when the order is paid, and a decrease is settled by the platform and carried to the next invoice.

items.q: Why does the price of my instance not change right away?
items.a: The recurring amount is lowered for the period that comes. The invoice of the current period is the price of the period that was paid.

title: Cancel an instance
summary: What happens to an instance when you cancel it, how long it is kept and what happens to your data.

items.title: Open the tab Settings
items.body: Open the instance and choose the tab Settings.
items.result: The name of the instance and the section Cancel instance are there.

items.title: Choose Cancel instance
items.body: The button is at the bottom of the panel. A dialog asks you to write the name of the instance to confirm.
items.result: The dialog says that the instance stops at the end of the paid period.

items.title: Confirm
items.body: Write the name of the instance and confirm.
items.result: The page says: Cancellation scheduled for the end of the paid period.

blocks.text: The instance keeps running until the end of the paid period, then it is removed. You can resume it from billing before then.
The subscription of the instance is set to end with the period that was paid. When the period is over, the instance is withdrawn and the subscription is not renewed.

A cancelled instance is kept for a term of retention, thirty days by default. The data of the instance is exported before anything is deleted, and the container itself is removed only when the term is over and the operator has allowed the automatic deletion.
The data of the instance is not gone when the period ends.

The export of the instance is written when the service is cancelled and it stays available after the service is deleted. The billing page lists the cancelled services and says whether the export is available.

The export describes the service and the records of the account: the name of the instance, its product, its limits, its price, its hostnames, its events, its invoices and its payments. It is not a copy of the files of the container — a copy of the files is a [backup](/docs?p=backups).

The panel Subscriptions of the billing page carries the action Cancel at period end for each instance. The dialog says that the instance keeps running until the date of the end of the period, then it is stopped and it is no longer billed.

items.q: Can I undo the cancellation?
items.a: Yes, as long as the period is not over: the subscription carries the action Resume on the billing page.

items.q: Are my files deleted when the period ends?
items.a: The instance is withdrawn when the period is over, and the data of the instance is exported. The container itself is removed when the term of retention is over and the operator has allowed the automatic deletion. Take a backup before you cancel if the files matter to you.

items.q: I want a refund.
items.a: The platform refunds a payment by itself when a service that was paid for could not be provisioned. A refund on request is decided by a person: see [Refunds and credits](/docs?p=refunds).

title: Refunds and credits
summary: When the platform returns a payment by itself, when a person decides, and what the platform does not do.

blocks.text: There are two cases where the money goes back without anybody having to ask for it:

items: A service that was paid for and could not be provisioned. The deployment failed, the order is marked as refunded and the payment provider is asked to return the amount. The event is written in the events of the instance.
A change of resources that was paid for and could not be applied. The change is refunded and the instance keeps the resources it had.

blocks.text: A refund that the provider itself refuses is flagged, and the operator returns the money by hand instead of the platform keeping a payment for a service that does not exist.

sections.title: The refunds that are decided by a person

blocks.text: Outside those two cases a refund is not automatic. A request is looked at by the operator and the decision is taken by a person.

items.title: Open a ticket
items.body: Open the menu Support and write to the team. Describe the service, the order and what you expect.
items.result: The ticket appears in the list of your tickets.

items.title: Wait for the answer
items.body: The team answers in the ticket.
items.result: The answer says what is done with the money.

blocks.text: The platform does not promise how long a refund takes. The payment provider states the delay.
A decrease of the resources is not refunded. The difference is carried to the next invoice of the account.

sections.title: What the platform does not do

items: It does not refund an order that was never paid: the change is simply not applied.
It does not refund a paid order twice: an order whose payment was already returned is never applied again and never refunded again.
It does not promise a refund that it has not implemented.

title: Attach a domain to an instance
summary: How to claim a hostname for an instance, prove that you own it, and take it back.

items.title: Open the instance
items.body: Go to the instance page and open the Domains tab.
items.result: The tab lists the hostnames this instance answers on.

items.title: Add the hostname
items.body: Add the hostname you want, without a scheme, for example app.example.com.
items.result: The hostname appears with a status and the records you have to publish.

items.title: Note the records
items.body: Every record shows a name, a type and a value.
items.result: You have everything you need for your DNS provider.

blocks.text: A hostname of the platform is reserved. apps.blipmade.com and everything under it belong to the platform, and a claim of one of them is refused.

A hostname is proved with a TXT record. The platform publishes nothing in your DNS zone: you create the records at your provider, and the platform reads them back to check. The name of the record is _blipmade-verify. followed by your hostname, and the value is a token of 24 characters that the platform made for this hostname. The token is different for every hostname and it is shown on the domain itself.

blocks.code:
; example only - copy the real name and the real token from the domain in your dashboard
_blipmade-verify.app.example.com   TXT   the 24 character token of the domain

blocks.text: An address record is not enough, because every customer points at the same address. The TXT record is what tells two hostnames apart.
A claim that is never proved runs out after seven days. After that the hostname is free again, and you have to claim it a second time.

items.title: Open the domain
items.body: The Domains page of the dashboard lists every hostname of your account.
items.result: You see its status, the records it needs and the proof it expects.

items.title: Publish the proof
items.body: Add the TXT record at your provider. The name and the value are on the domain itself, under the label Prove that you own this hostname.
items.result: Your provider shows the record.

items.title: Verify now
items.body: Press Verify now. The platform reads the TXT record and compares it with the token of the domain.
items.result: The status moves from Verifying to Active.

items.title: Open the hostname
items.body: Visit your own hostname in a browser.
items.result: Your instance answers on the hostname you chose.

blocks.text: The platform also sends you a mail with the name and the value of the proof when you claim the hostname, so you can publish it without coming back to the dashboard.

rows.v: The platform is checking the TXT record.
The hostname is not routed yet: either the proof was not accepted, or the route could not be written.
The hostname is proved and the platform is still writing its route to the gateway.
The hostname is proved and routed to your instance.
The last attempt failed. The domain shows the last error it hit.

blocks.text: A hostname that was never proved is never routed. Nothing of the platform answers on it, whatever your DNS says.

items.title: Open the domain
items.body: The Domains page lists every hostname of your account.
items.result: You see the hostname.

items.title: Delete it
items.body: Press Delete and type the hostname to confirm.
items.result: The hostname is removed from your account.

blocks.text: The hostname stops resolving as soon as you delete it. This cannot be undone, and the proof of the hostname goes with it.

sections.title: When the hostname does not work

items.q: The status stays Verifying
items.a: The TXT record is not visible yet or does not carry the expected value. Wait for the DNS to spread and verify again. If the claim runs out after seven days, claim the hostname again.

items.q: The status turns to Error
items.a: The domain shows the last error it hit. Compare the records at your provider with the records the domain lists, character by character.

items.q: The hostname resolves but the site is empty
items.a: The instance is stopped or is not listening on the port of the domain. Check the status and the target port of the domain.

items.q: The hostname worked and stopped working
items.a: The routes of the customers live in the configuration of the gateway, and a restart of the gateway takes them away. The platform writes them back every minute, so a hostname that stays dead for more than a few minutes is a problem to report.

title: The DNS records you need
summary: Which records to publish at your DNS provider, and where to read their values.

blocks.text: Every domain in your dashboard lists the records it expects, each with a name, a type and a value. Blipmade does not guess them and it does not write them: it tells you what to create at your DNS provider, because the DNS of your domain belongs to you.

items: An A record for the bare hostname, with the address of the gateway of the platform.
A CNAME record for www, pointing at the bare hostname. The platform asks for this one name only. A subdomain of your own is not routed until you claim it and prove it on its own.
A TXT record that proves the hostname belongs to you, published under _blipmade-verify. followed by the hostname, with the token of the domain.
Nothing else. Do not add a second A record for the same name, because the resolver has to pick one.

blocks.code:
; example only - copy the real values from the domain in your dashboard
app.example.com                      A       203.0.113.10
www.app.example.com                  CNAME   app.example.com
_blipmade-verify.app.example.com      TXT     the 24 character token of the domain

blocks.text: If your provider has a CNAME flattening or a proxy setting, turn it off for these records. A proxied hostname does not answer the verification check.

items.title: Open the domain in the dashboard
items.body: The list of records is on the domain itself.
items.result: You see the name, the type and the value of each record.

items.title: Create them at your provider
items.body: Add one record per line, exactly as listed.
items.result: Your provider shows the new records.

items.title: Verify
items.body: Start the verification again from the domain page.
items.result: The status becomes Active once the records are visible.

blocks.text: Propagation is the time between creating a record and every resolver seeing it. It is usually minutes and at worst a few hours, and it depends on the TTL of your record rather than on Blipmade.
A claim that is never proved runs out after seven days, so verify again as soon as your records are published.

sections.title: The records of a mail domain

blocks.text: A domain of mail needs other records: the mail server that has to receive the mail, the signature of the domain and the two records that let a mail client find its settings by itself. They are listed on the domain itself in the Email page of the dashboard, and they are described in [the DNS records of a mail domain](/docs?p=mail-dns).
A hostname that carries both an instance and a mail domain needs both sets of records. Publish them one after the other and check each of them where it belongs.

title: SSL certificates
summary: Where HTTPS on a hostname of yours stands today: the platform issues no certificate.

blocks.text: An automatic certificate for a hostname you attach to an instance is {{planned}}. The route the platform writes for a hostname is a plain forward to your container: it carries no certificate. The platform does not issue one and it does not ask you to upload one either, so a hostname of yours is served over plain HTTP today.
The certificate of blipmade.com covers the addresses of the platform only. It says nothing about a hostname you attach to an instance.

The dashboard keeps no certificate and no TLS state for a domain, because the platform holds none. The domain answer carries the hostname, the status, the target port, the records and the last error, and nothing else.

items.title: Do not treat the hostname as a secure channel
items.body: The platform terminates no TLS for a hostname of a customer, so a password or a token that travels through it travels in clear text.
items.result: You know what the hostname is good for.

items.title: Keep the sensitive part behind a proxy of your own
items.body: If your application has an admin area, put a proxy of your own in front of the instance, with your own certificate for a hostname your proxy owns, and reach the admin area through that hostname. The hostname the platform routes stays the plain way in, because the platform is the one that routes it.
items.result: The admin area is reached over HTTPS, through your own proxy.

items.title: Protect the application itself
items.body: Set a strong password for the application and for its admin area before you expose the instance.
items.result: A guessable admin account is no longer the weakest link.

blocks.code:
# check how your own hostname answers today
curl -I http://app.example.com

blocks.text: The certificate of the platform covers the names of the platform and nothing else. It does not cover a hostname under the domain of the platform, and it does not cover a hostname of yours. A certificate you get for a hostname from your own provider does not protect it either, because the platform answers on that hostname itself.
Nothing in the dashboard tells you that a certificate is on its way: the domain answer carries no certificate and no TLS state. Treat the automatic certificate of a hostname as not available.

title: The domain of the platform
summary: What apps.blipmade.com is, how it differs from a domain of yours, and which address your instance gets.

blocks.text: The platform has one domain of its own: apps.blipmade.com. It is the base under which the platform reserves its names, and it is not yours to claim. The claim of the base, and of anything under it, is refused with the message That hostname is reserved by the platform.

rows.v: apps.blipmade.com. It is reserved, and a claim of it or of anything under it is refused.
The address and the port the panel assigned to the instance. It is shown in the Network tab of the instance.
A hostname of a domain you own. You claim it on the instance page and you prove that it is yours.

items.title: Open the instance
items.body: Go to the instance page and open the Network tab.
items.result: The tab shows the addresses of the instance.

items.title: Find the primary one
items.body: The panel assigns an address to every server, and the primary one is the address the service is reached at.
items.result: You have the address and the port of your instance.

items.title: Read it as it is
items.body: The address is an IP address and a port. It is not a name, and it carries no certificate.
items.result: You know what the address of an instance can and cannot do.

sections.title: A hostname under the domain of the platform

blocks.text: A hostname under apps.blipmade.com is a name of the platform. The platform keeps the name and its zone, and it reserves the whole base, so no account can claim one. Today no route of an instance is published under that base: every hostname of a customer is a hostname of a domain the customer owns.

The difference is who proves the ownership and who is responsible for the DNS. For a hostname of your own, you publish the records at your provider and you prove that the hostname is yours; the platform then routes it to your instance and keeps the route up. For a name of the platform, the platform is the owner and nobody has to prove anything.
A hostname of yours that is claimed for an instance is described in [Attach a domain to an instance](/docs?p=domains), and the records it needs are in [The DNS records you need](/docs?p=dns).

The certificate of blipmade.com covers the addresses of the platform, so the dashboard and the site are reached over HTTPS. It covers neither a hostname under apps.blipmade.com nor a hostname of yours. The details are in [SSL certificates](/docs?p=ssl).

title: Browse and edit files
summary: What the file browser of an instance can do, and what it cannot do for you.

items.title: Open the instance
items.body: Go to the files section of the instance.
items.result: You see the files of the instance root.

items.title: Walk into a folder
items.body: Open folders to see what is inside, and go back with the breadcrumb.
items.result: You see the files with their size and their last modification.

items.title: Open the file
items.body: Open a text file to see its content.
items.result: The content is shown in an editor.

items.title: Change it and save
items.body: Edit the content and press Save file.
items.result: The file on the instance holds the new content.

blocks.text: Saving replaces the whole file. If the application is running and holds it open, it may keep working with the old content until it is restarted.

The browser also renames a file, moves or copies it into another folder of the same instance, and changes its permissions. A file that is not text is not shown in the editor: download it and change it outside.
The Folders panel of the browser has an Upload button, and every file has a Download action. The upload goes to the folder that is open in the panel.
The file browser is meant for configuration and small edits. For large uploads, use the console: a download in the instance is faster and does not depend on the browser.

items.title: Select the file
items.body: Open the folder that holds the file.
items.result: The file is listed with its size.

items.title: Delete it
items.body: Press Delete and confirm. The browser warns that the file is removed from the instance and that this cannot be undone.
items.result: The file is removed from the instance.

blocks.text: There is no trash folder, and nothing takes a copy of the file for you. Take a [backup](/docs?p=backups) before you delete something.

sections.title: What the browser does not do

items: It does not show anything outside the container of the instance. The browser is the door to the container and to nothing else.
It does not keep a copy of anything. A file you delete is gone from the instance, and a file you change is changed for good.
It does not replace the console. A command that installs something belongs in the console or in the startup command of the instance.

title: Open the console
summary: A shell on the instance, straight from the dashboard, and what it is for.

items.title: Open the instance
items.body: Go to the console section of the instance.
items.result: The console connects and shows the output of the application.

items.title: Wait for a prompt
items.body: The console attaches to the process of the instance as the user the application runs as.
items.result: You can type commands.

blocks.text: The browser asks the platform for the console, and the platform opens it on the server with the key of your account. The key never reaches the browser.

items: Reading the output of the application when it will not start.
Running migrations, imports or a one-off script inside the instance.
Checking what is actually on disk, including files the browser does not show.
Moving a large file in or out of the container, faster than through the browser.

blocks.text: The console shows the output as it arrives. The browser keeps the last lines it received and the platform keeps no history of them: a reload of the page loses the output, and a restart of the instance loses it for good. The details are in [The logs of a service](/docs?p=logs).

sections.title: What the console does not do

items: It does not give you the privileges of the platform. You cannot manage other instances or the billing from inside the console.
It does not survive a rebuild of the instance. Anything you installed outside your project is gone after the next rebuild.
It does not replace a backup. Keep your own copy of what matters.

blocks.text: Put anything you want to run on every start into the startup command of the instance. The console is for the one-off job.

title: The logs of a service
summary: Where the output of an application comes from, what the platform keeps of it, and what you have to keep yourself.

blocks.text: The output of your application is written by the process that runs in the container. The console of the instance shows it while it is produced, and that is the only place the platform shows it to you.
The platform does not collect the logs of your application. There is no log page in the dashboard, no log file is written for you and no history of the output is kept.

rows.v: The Activity tab of the instance records what the platform did with it: it was built, started, stopped, resized or renamed. The last hundred of those steps are kept.
The same tab shows the activity that the panel recorded on the server of the instance.
Nothing. It is only in the console of the moment.

items.title: Write the log where you want it
items.body: Ask your application to write its own log to a file in the container, for example in the folder of the project.
items.result: The log is a file of the instance.

items.title: Read or download it
items.body: Open the file in the file browser of the instance, or download it.
items.result: You have a copy that survives a restart of the instance.

items.title: Put it in a backup
items.body: Ask for a backup of the instance and download it.
items.result: The log is in the archive together with the rest of the files.

blocks.text: A file you write yourself is a file of the container: it is in the backup and in the file browser. The platform does not keep a log for you and does not rotate it.

sections.title: When you need the output of a crash

items.q: The instance stopped and the output is gone
items.a: The output of the process went with the process. Restart the instance and read the console: the lines of the new start are what the platform can still show you.

items.q: The console opens but shows nothing
items.a: The instance is stopped. Start it from the instance page and open the console again.

items.q: I need the output of an incident of yesterday
items.a: The platform keeps no history of the output. Take the output yourself in the file your application writes, and put a backup of the instance around it.

title: Account security
summary: Your password, your sessions and the mail of your account.

blocks.text: Signing in creates a session on the server and hands the browser an HttpOnly cookie. Scripts in the page cannot read it. The session lasts fourteen days from the moment you signed in, and your activity does not make it last longer.
After fourteen days the session ends on its own and you sign in again. You can end it earlier from the Sessions panel of the settings page, one session at a time.

items.title: Open the settings
items.body: Go to the Settings page of your account and open the Sessions panel.
items.result: You see every session that is open, with the browser and the system it runs on.

items.title: Read the line of a session
items.body: The line shows the address of the session, the moment you signed in and the last activity of that session. The session you are on is marked This device.
items.result: You know which session is the one in front of you.

items.title: Close the ones you do not want
items.body: Press Close session on the session you do not recognise, or Close the other sessions to end every session but this one.
items.result: The session ends on the server at once, and the cookie of that browser stops working.

blocks.code:
# the sessions that are open for your account
curl -X GET "$BASE/api/settings/sessions" -b cookies.txt

items.title: Open the Password panel
items.body: The settings page of your account has a Password panel.
items.result: The form asks for the current password and for the new one, twice.

items.title: Choose a password of ten characters or more
items.body: The password needs at least ten characters, with a lowercase letter, an uppercase letter and a digit.
items.result: The form refuses a password that does not have them.

items.title: Save it
items.body: Press Change the password.
items.result: The password is changed and the other sessions of the account end. The device you are on stays signed in.

blocks.text: Changing the password closes the other sessions of the account, and a script that holds your cookie stops working at the same moment.

When you cannot sign in, the password is reset with a link that the platform mails to the address of the account. The reset link opens the reset page of the platform with a token in it, not the settings page.

items.title: Ask for a reset link
items.body: Open the forgot password page, which is linked from the sign-in page.
items.result: The platform emails a link to the address on the account.

items.title: Open the link
items.body: The link opens the reset page with the token of the request.
items.result: The page switches to the new password form.

items.title: Choose the new password
items.body: Enter the new password twice and confirm. The new password needs ten characters, a lowercase letter, an uppercase letter and a digit.
items.result: You are signed out of the old session and the new password works from now on.

blocks.code:
# the API answers the same way either way, so nobody can learn whether the address exists
# and it says whether the message could really be sent
curl -X POST "$BASE/api/auth/forgot-password" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email":"you@example.com"}'

items.title: Open the verification email
items.body: The link in the email carries a token that verifies the address.
items.result: The account shows the address as verified.

items.title: Request a new email if it expired
items.body: Ask for a new verification email on the registration page or on the verification page of the address. There is no control for it in the dashboard.
items.result: A new link arrives. The answer is the same whether or not the address exists.

blocks.text: Signing out ends the session on the server and clears the cookie in the browser. The settings page has a button for it, and the Sessions panel signs out the device you are on.

title: Instance access and secrets
summary: How you reach an instance, where its environment is read, and why there are no keys.

items: The file browser of the dashboard reads and writes the files of the container. It is described in [Browse and edit files](/docs?p=files).
The console of the dashboard runs commands in the container. It is described in [Open the console](/docs?p=console).

The panel that runs the instances offers an SFTP access to the container on node1.blipmade.com:2022. The platform does not manage that access and does not show it in the dashboard, so it is not something your account carries.

blocks.text: Everything you do to an instance goes through the account you signed in with. The credential of the platform stays on the server, in your account only.

items.title: Open the instance
items.body: Go to the startup and environment section of the instance.
items.result: You see the current variables and the startup command.

items.title: Set the variables
items.body: Add or change the variables the application needs and save.
items.result: The environment of the server holds the new values.

items.title: Wait for the next start
items.body: Saving the environment does not restart the instance. The values that are running are the ones the instance had when it started.
items.result: The new values are in place after the next start.

blocks.text: Environment variables are readable by anyone who can open the instance and by everything that runs inside it. Keep tokens and database passwords out of your code.
The startup command is what the instance runs when it starts. Put your migrations and your installs in it, so a restart comes back in a working state. Saving it does not restart the instance either.

blocks.code: npm ci --include=dev && npm run build && npm run migrate && exec node server.mjs

blocks.text: The API lives under /api of the same address you use for the dashboard. Requests are same-origin and carry your session cookie. Every request that changes something also needs the X-CSRF-Token header, whose value is the readable bm_csrf cookie.

blocks.code:
# read the token out of the cookie jar
CSRF=$(awk '/bm_csrf/ {print $7}' cookies.txt)

curl -X POST "$BASE/api/tickets" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-CSRF-Token: $CSRF" \
  -b cookies.txt \
  -d '{"subject":"The instance does not answer","category":"technical","priority":"normal","body":"The console shows nothing after the restart."}'

blocks.text: Programmatic keys are {{planned}}. The API does not expose key management, so the dashboard does not offer a button to create one. Until then, scripts use the session of an account, which means they need the cookie and the CSRF token of a signed-in user.
Do not put the session cookie of a real account into a script that runs unattended. Treat every cookie like a password.

title: Who can do what
summary: What your account can do in the dashboard, and how the back office of the platform is split.

blocks.text: Everything in the dashboard belongs to the account you signed in with. The instances, the hostnames, the tickets, the subscriptions and the files are checked against the owner on every request, and an instance of somebody else answers like an instance that does not exist.
There is no second level of permission in the customer area. An account that can open an instance can read its files, run commands in it, change its environment, take a backup of it and remove it.

items: Open, change and remove your own instances, and start and stop them.
Claim a hostname for one of them, prove that it is yours and remove it again.
Read and write the files of your instances, run commands in them and take a backup of them.
Open a support ticket, attach one of your instances to it and read the answers.
Change the password, the mail address and the sessions of your account, and close your account.

sections.title: The roles of the back office

blocks.text: The staff of the platform works in a back office that is separate from the customer area. It has two roles.

rows.v: Holds every permission of the platform.
Holds only the permissions that were granted to that person.

blocks.text: Every permission comes in two: one to read and one to write. The areas are the customers, the orders, the services, the catalog, the prices, the tickets, the promotions, the infrastructure, the mail, the audit log, the staff and the settings of the platform.

A staff member who does not hold a permission cannot hand it out either: nobody can grant more than they hold. The access to the container of a customer always goes through the credential of the customer, so the staff of the platform never reaches your files with its own privileges.

items.q: I see an instance, a hostname or a ticket that is not mine
items.a: Everything the dashboard shows belongs to the account you signed in with. If a page shows something of somebody else, sign out and open a ticket: it is a fault of the platform, not something you are allowed to see.

items.q: A colleague needs the same instance
items.a: There is no second user on an account. Every person who needs access needs an account of their own, and every account owns its own instances.

items.q: I lost the session of a device and I do not know which one
items.a: The Sessions panel of the settings page lists every session with its address and its last activity. Close the one you do not recognise, or close the other sessions at once. The details are in [Account security](/docs?p=account-security).

title: Email hosting
summary: What the hosted mail of the platform is, and that it is not on sale today.

blocks.text: The hosted mail is not on sale today, so no plan of hosted mail can be bought and no mail service can be started.
Do not expect a mail plan, a mail domain or a mailbox that you can order today. So that you know what you are waiting for, here is what the feature holds. Nothing of it can be bought today.

items: A mail domain of your own, with the DNS records that make the mail arrive there.
Mailboxes on that domain, each with a password, a space of its own and a sending limit.
Aliases: addresses that deliver into a mailbox instead of being a mailbox of their own.
The webmail of the platform, where the mail of the domain is read.
A suspension of the whole mail service, with a period of grace before the mail stops.

blocks.text: A plan of hosted mail sets a number of domains, a number of mailboxes per domain, a number of aliases per domain, a number of forwarding rules per domain, the space of the plan, the space of one mailbox and a sending limit. The Email page of the dashboard shows these limits for each plan, and shows that the plan is not on sale yet.
The plans carry no price yet. A price that nobody decided is not an offer, so none is written here either.

items.title: Use the mail of the platform
items.body: The address of your account receives the notifications of the account: the verification of the address, the change of the password, the state of your tickets and the life of your instances.
items.result: The messages of the platform reach you by mail.

items.title: Keep that address in good order
items.body: The address of the account is changed in the Profile panel of the settings page, and the change is only made when you open the link of the confirmation mail.
items.result: The notifications keep reaching an address you read.

items.title: Decide what you want to hear
items.body: The groups of the messages are switched in the Notifications panel of the settings page.
items.result: You receive the messages you asked for. The details are in [Notifications](/docs?p=notifications).

blocks.text: The hosted mail of the platform is a different thing from the mail of the platform. The second one is the channel of your account; the first one is a service you would buy, and it is not for sale.

title: Mailboxes and aliases
summary: What a mailbox of a mail domain is, what an alias does, and the space a mailbox may use.

blocks.text: Hosted mail is not on sale today, so there is no mail domain and no mailbox in your account today. Here is what you get when the sale opens.
A mailbox is an address that receives mail and that you open in the webmail or in a mail client. It has a password, a space of its own and a status.

rows.v: The address of the mailbox, for example info@example.com.
Active, or Disabled when the mail system has turned it off.
How much of the space of the mailbox is used, for example 12 MB of 1024 MB.
Yours to choose, with at least ten characters. The platform makes one when you bring none, and shows it once.

blocks.text: The password of a mailbox is shown once, when the mailbox is created. It is not written down anywhere else, so a lost password means a new mailbox.

An alias is an address that delivers into a mailbox instead of being a mailbox of its own. It is the way to have info@ and support@ reach the same mailbox, and the way to publish an address without opening it.

An alias points at one mailbox, and the dashboard shows that mailbox in the column Goes to. When the mailbox goes, the aliases that deliver to it go with it: the mail system removes them, because an alias that the platform shows and the mail system does not have is an alias that delivers nowhere.
A domain of mail has a space of its own and its mailboxes share it. The plan sets both: the space of the plan and the space of one mailbox.

sections.title: The suspension of a mail service

blocks.text: The mail service is suspended as a whole, not mailbox by mailbox. When the service is cancelled it goes through a period of grace, and it is suspended when the grace ends. The data of the service is kept through the grace and after the suspension, and the service can be brought back while it is not cancelled.

items.q: I lost the password of a mailbox
items.a: The platform keeps no copy of it: the mail system keeps only its hash and the password was shown once, in the answer of the request that created the mailbox. Delete the mailbox and create it again with a password you choose.

items.q: The status of a mailbox is Disabled
items.a: The status comes from the mail system and not from the dashboard. A disabled mailbox does not take any new mail.

items.q: The domain of mail receives nothing
items.a: The records of the domain are not published yet, or the mail of the domain is not delivered to it. Check the records in the Email page: the platform reads them and tells you which ones are missing.

title: The DNS records of a mail domain
summary: The records a domain of mail needs, what each of them is for, and how the platform checks them.

blocks.text: Hosted mail is not on sale today, so there is no domain of mail in your account today. Here are the records it needs.
A domain of mail needs six kinds of record. The Email page of the dashboard lists them with the value to publish and a line that says what each of them is for.

items: An MX record for the domain itself, pointing at the mail server of the platform, with the priority 10. It is where the mail addressed to this domain is delivered.
A TXT record for the domain itself, with the value v=spf1 mx -all. It says that only this mail server may send mail for this domain.
A TXT record for _dmarc. followed by the domain. It says what to do with the mail that does not pass the checks.
A CNAME record for autodiscover. followed by the domain, pointing at the mail server. It lets a mail client find the settings of the mailbox by itself.
A CNAME record for autoconfig. followed by the domain, pointing at the mail server. It lets a mail client set itself up by itself.

A TXT record for dkim._domainkey. followed by the domain, with the key of the domain. It signs the mail of the domain, so that it is not read as a forgery. The record is only listed once the mail system has made the key.

sections.title: The platform does not write them

blocks.text: The platform does not write these records. The DNS of a domain belongs to the customer, so the platform tells you what to publish and then checks, with a real lookup, what is really published. A record that the platform would write itself could overwrite something that you need.

items.title: Open the Email page
items.body: The domain of mail lists the records it needs and, next to each of them, what is really published.
items.result: You see which records are missing.

items.title: Publish what is missing
items.body: Add the records at your provider, exactly as listed, with the same names and the same values.
items.result: Your provider shows them.

items.title: Check again
items.body: Ask the page for the state of the records again. The check is made when you ask for it and not on a timer.
items.result: The domain is delivered once the records are published.

sections.title: The difference with the records of an instance

blocks.text: These records have nothing to do with the records of an instance. An instance needs an address record and a proof of ownership; a domain of mail needs the records above. A hostname that carries both needs both sets. The records of an instance are in [The DNS records you need](/docs?p=dns).

title: The webmail and the mail clients
summary: Where the mail of a domain is read, and what a mail client is given to read it.

blocks.text: Hosted mail is not on sale today, so there is no domain of mail and no mailbox in your account today. Here is what you get when the sale opens.

The webmail is where the mail of a domain is read, in the browser. The address comes from the platform, and the page says when there is no webmail set up instead of showing an address that does not work.

A mail client needs the settings of the mailbox: the host of the incoming and the outgoing server, and the ports they listen on. The platform does not publish them today, so a client cannot be set up from the dashboard alone.

The records of the domain are what makes it possible for a client to find those settings by itself: the autodiscover and the autoconfig records point a client at the mail server of the platform. They are described in [The DNS records of a mail domain](/docs?p=mail-dns).
If you need the settings of a mail client and they are not published, open a ticket and say which client and which domain you use.

items.title: Open the Email page
items.body: The domain of mail shows the webmail of the platform.
items.result: You have the link to the webmail.

items.title: Sign in with the mailbox
items.body: Sign in with the address and the password of the mailbox.
items.result: The mail of the mailbox is shown.

items.title: Or use a mail client
items.body: Set your client up with the settings of the platform and the address of the mailbox.
items.result: Your client fetches the same mail as the webmail.

title: Notifications
summary: What the platform tells you, where it reaches you, and how to switch a group of messages off.

blocks.text: The platform tells you two ways, and both carry the same messages.

items: The notification centre: the bell of the dashboard opens the Notifications page, where the messages of your account are listed with their group and their date. You can mark a message as read and you can delete it.
The mail: the same messages reach the address of your account, unless you switch the mail off for that group.

blocks.text: The two are one setting on the server: switching one of them off stops the whole group.

rows.v: The verification of the address, the change of the password, the change of the address. They are always sent, because they protect the account.
Your orders, your payments and your invoices. The notice about a payment that failed and the notice about an invoice that is late are always sent.
The life of your servers: they are built, they work, they are suspended.
Your tickets: a new answer, a change of state, a closing.
Your domains and the hosted mail: the proof of ownership, the records of DNS, the mailboxes.
An incident of the platform and the work that is planned.
The platform itself: what is new, what changed, what is planned.
The offers of the platform. They are off until you agree to them.

items.title: Open the settings
items.body: Go to the Settings page of your account and open the Notifications panel.
items.result: The panel lists the groups of the messages and the channels they travel on.

items.title: Switch the group off
items.body: Untick the channel of the group you do not want to hear from.
items.result: The switch is saved and the group stops reaching you.

items.title: Leave the account group on
items.body: The group that protects the account is marked Always on and offers no switch. Those messages keep coming whatever you tick.
items.result: The messages that protect the account are never lost.

blocks.code:
# the five groups of the old preferences, read and written as one object
curl -X PUT "$BASE/api/settings/notifications" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-CSRF-Token: $CSRF" \
  -b cookies.txt \
  -d '{"productUpdates":false,"billing":true,"support":true,"incidents":true,"marketing":false}'

blocks.text: The marketing is off until you agree to it. Turning it on is your agreement to receive the offers of the platform by mail, and every one of them carries a way to stop them. The date of your agreement is kept, and switching the group off again takes it away.

sections.title: What the platform will not turn off

items.q: I switched a group off and I still get the messages
items.a: The messages of a group that is marked Always on are always sent. The group that protects the account is the one that stays on, whatever you switch.

items.q: I get a message that I do not recognize
items.a: The Notifications page lists every message with its group. The group tells you what the message is about: a ticket, an order, an instance or your account.

items.q: I do not receive any mail at all
items.a: Check the address of the account in the Profile panel of the settings page, and check the spam folder of that address: the messages of the platform come from the mail server of the platform.

title: Backups of an instance
summary: The archive of the files of an instance, how to take it, how to restore it, and what it does not hold.

blocks.text: A backup is an archive of the files of the container of an instance. The panel writes it on the node where the instance runs. It is a file and not a history: the platform keeps no list of the backups you took in the past and no copy of one after you delete it.
It is manual. Nothing makes one on a schedule: you ask for a backup and the panel writes one in the background. There is no automatic backup of your instance today.
The copy the platform keeps of its own database is not a backup of your application and not a backup of your files. Take your own copy from the [Backups](/docs?p=backups) page.

items.title: Open the instance
items.body: Go to the instance page and open the Backups tab.
items.result: You see the backups of the instance, or a panel that says there are none yet.

items.title: Ask for one
items.body: Press New backup and give it a name.
items.result: The dashboard says the backup was asked for and that the panel writes it in the background.

items.title: Wait for it
items.body: The backup appears in the list with its size and the moment it was written.
items.result: The backup is ready to download.

blocks.code:
# ask the platform for an archive of the files of the container
curl -X POST "$BASE/api/instances/$INSTANCE/backups" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-CSRF-Token: $CSRF" \
  -b cookies.txt \
  -d '{"name":"before-the-change","locked":false}'

items.title: Download it
items.body: Press Download on the backup.
items.result: You get a .tar.gz archive of the files of the container.

items.title: Restore it
items.body: Press Restore and confirm. The dashboard warns you that the files of the container are replaced by the archive and that what is in the container now and is not in the backup is lost.
items.result: The files of the container are the files of the archive.

items.title: Keep the copy
items.body: Download the backup and keep it where your own backups live.
items.result: The archive on the node is not the only copy, because the platform keeps no history of it.

sections.title: What a backup does not hold

items: Nothing outside the container. A database that runs on another machine, a file on your own computer and an object store are not in the archive.
Nothing of the platform. The archive holds the files of your instance and nothing else.

blocks.text: The database of your own application is inside the container, so it is part of the backup: the archive holds every file of the container, the data directory of the database included. What is not in the archive is what lives outside the container.
A restore replaces the files of the container with the archive. A file that was written after the archive was taken is not in it, and the restore loses it.

items.title: Take one before a change
items.body: Take a backup before you change something in the container by hand and before you reinstall the instance.
items.result: There is an archive of the files as they were before the change.

items.title: Download it
items.body: A backup stays on the node until you delete it. Download the ones you want to keep.
items.result: The copy is yours and not only on the node.

items.title: Take one regularly, by hand
items.body: Nothing takes a backup for you on a schedule, so the last one is the one you made.
items.result: You know how old your copy is.

items.q: The backup did not appear
items.a: The panel writes the archive in the background. Wait a moment and reload the list. If it never appears, open a ticket with the name of the backup.

items.q: The restore did not bring my file back
items.a: A restore replaces the files of the container with the archive. If the file was written after the backup was taken, it is not in the archive and it is gone.

items.q: How many backups can I keep
items.a: The number of backups is the limit of the panel, and the platform sets no limit of its own and no term of its own. The Backups tab shows the ones you have.

title: Common problems
summary: What to check, in the order that usually finds the cause.

sections.title: Check the state of the instance

items.title: Look at the state
items.body: Open the instance. The state is shown next to its name, and the Overview tab tells you what it may use against what it uses right now.
items.result: You see whether it is Pending, Provisioning, Online, Restarting, Stopped, Failed, Suspended or Cancelled, and how much memory, disk and processor it uses.

items.title: Start it if it is stopped
items.body: Use the Start action of the instance. It is offered when the instance is Stopped or Failed.
items.result: The container is started again and the state follows it.

items.title: Read the console
items.body: Open the Console tab. It shows the output of the application, and the reason it did not start is written there.
items.result: You see the error that stopped the application, in the words of the program itself.

blocks.text: The state you read is the real state of the container: when it reads Online, your container is answering.

The Overview tab shows the memory, the disk and the processor of the instance against the limits it was given, and the state of the container. An application that asks for more memory than the limit of the container is stopped by the container itself; that is the usual reason an instance that worked yesterday is stopped today.
The disk of an instance is one disk. The database, the logs and the uploads end up on the same one, and a full disk stops the application.
Give the application the memory it needs. When the memory of the instance sits at its limit, raise Memory in the Resources tab of the instance.
The Activity tab records what happened to the instance: when it was started, stopped, resized or renamed. It is the fastest way to see whether something changed on our side.

If the instance stopped on its own and the payment method is old, the subscription may be past due. An invoice that was not paid puts the subscription in Past due, and after a grace of seven days the instance is stopped and marked Suspended. The data is kept while it is suspended.
The Billing page shows the state of every subscription and lets you update the card. It also shows the state of every invoice, so you never have to ask where a payment stands.

Still stuck? Open a ticket and attach the instance. Include what you expected, what happened, and the relevant part of the console output. That context is what makes the difference between a question and an answer. The page [Support tickets](/docs?p=tickets) describes the ticket in full.
If the problem is the platform and not your instance, the [status page](/docs?p=status) says whether other customers are seeing it too.

sections.title: Problems that do not happen yet

blocks.text: Some problems are heard a lot but do not exist in the platform today. They are written here so nobody looks for them.

items: There is no metrics page. The dashboard has no page of metrics, and the numbers of the instance are read in the Overview tab of the instance, against the limits it was given.

An instance is never shown as degraded because it is short of memory. The platform writes the state the container is really in; an application that wants more memory than the limit is stopped by the container, and the console says so.
There is no page of the uptime history. The status page shows the state of the moment and no history of it.
No answer time is published for a ticket, so a ticket that waits is not a fault of the platform.

title: Support
summary: How to reach the operator, what the operator can and cannot do, and what to write in a ticket so the answer comes quickly.
